name: A ROMA WITH A VIEW BURGER

recipe.history:
The Roma tomato — also known as the plum tomato or paste tomato — is a variety of Solanum lycopersicum developed through agricultural selection in the Italian-American tomato canning industry of the mid-20th century, building on older Italian plum tomato cultivars. The tomato itself originated in western South America, where wild species of Solanum were cultivated by indigenous peoples of the Andes, Mesoamerica, and Mexico long before European contact. Spanish colonizers brought the tomato to Europe in the 16th century, where it was initially regarded with deep suspicion — as a member of the nightshade family, early Europeans feared it was poisonous — but Italian and Spanish cooks embraced it with enthusiasm, and southern Italy in particular developed the tomato culture that eventually gave the world marinara, pizza, and the San Marzano variety that remains the gold standard of Italian culinary tradition. The Roma variety was specifically bred for a lower water content, thicker walls, fewer seeds, and a more concentrated flavor than slicing tomatoes, making it ideal for cooking down into sauces and jams. When slow-roasted, the Roma's concentrated sugars caramelize into a jammy, intensely flavored result that is unlike the raw tomato in almost every respect.

Slow-roasted tomatoes entered American restaurant cooking via the New American and Mediterranean-influenced cuisine movements of the 1980s and 1990s. Chefs discovered that a low oven — 275 to 300 degrees Fahrenheit for one to three hours — transformed ordinary Roma tomatoes into something approaching a condiment of sun-dried intensity but with a different character: more jammy than leathery, more caramelized than tart. Tomato jam, pushed further — cooked with sugar, vinegar, and aromatics — is an extension of this principle, producing something that functions simultaneously as a sweet condiment, a savory sauce, and a structural flavor anchor. The combination of slow-roasted Romas as a topping and tomato jam as a spread doubles the tomato presence on this burger, using the vegetable in two completely different textural and flavor registers: concentrated and chewy in the roasted form, smooth and intensely fruity in the jam.

I spent a summer in a rented house with an oven that ran 25 degrees cold, which I discovered only after three weeks of confusing baking results. By the time I figured out the calibration problem, I had also discovered that slow-roasting Roma tomatoes in that cold oven for much longer than any recipe specified — three hours at what I thought was 275°F but was actually 250°F — produced the most extraordinary result I had ever seen from a tomato: concentrated, slightly chewy at the edges, jammy at the center, with a sweetness and depth that bore no resemblance to the raw fruit. I ate them on bread with burrata that evening and had to consciously stop myself from eating all of them before the rest of the meal. The tomato jam came the following week, from a surplus of Romas from the farmers' market and a desire to find something to do with them that would last longer than a salad.

The philosophy of this burger is the philosophy of patience applied to temperature — in the tomatoes and in the patty. The slow-roasted Romas demand hours. The medium-rare patty demands precision. Both are arguments against rushing, against excess heat, against overcooking. A Roma tomato slow-roasted at the correct temperature develops flavors that cannot be achieved in twenty minutes at high heat; a beef patty cooked to medium rare at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit retains moisture, fat, and complexity that disappear at higher temperatures. The tomato jam's sweetness and acidity need the richness of a properly pink, fat-saturated interior to balance them — a well-done patty would make the jam taste like it was sitting on cardboard. Every element of this burger rewards the cook who understands that restraint and patience are not weaknesses but techniques.
ingredients: 1/3 cup extra-virgin olive oil, plus more for pan
Flaky sea salt and freshly cracked black pepper
instructions: 1. Slow-roast the Roma tomatoes (start 3 hours before serving): Preheat oven to 275°F. Arrange halved Roma tomatoes cut-side up on a rimmed baking sheet. Tuck garlic slices, thyme, and rosemary between them. Drizzle with olive oil and balsamic vinegar; sprinkle with brown sugar, flaky salt, and pepper. Roast 2.5–3 hours until tomatoes are shrunken, concentrated, and jammy at the edges but still holding their shape. Cool slightly.

2. Make the tomato jam: Combine chopped Roma tomatoes, sugar, cider vinegar, lemon juice and zest, red pepper flakes, coriander, ginger, and salt in a medium saucepan. Bring to a boil, stirring, then reduce heat to medium-low. Cook, stirring frequently, 45–60 minutes until thick, jammy, and reduced by about half. It should mound on a spoon. Cool; refrigerate until needed.

3. Make the focaccia buns: Bloom yeast in warm water with sugar for 5 minutes. Combine flour, salt, and olive oil in a stand mixer; add yeast mixture; knead with dough hook 8 minutes. Cover; rise 1 hour. Oil a 9x13-inch pan generously; press dough in. Dimple with fingers; drizzle with olive oil, scatter thyme, rosemary, and flaky salt. Proof 45 minutes. Bake at 425°F for 18–22 minutes until golden. Cut into 6 squares; halve horizontally.
4. Quick-pickle red onion: Combine red wine vinegar, sugar, and salt. Add sliced red onion; toss. Macerate 20+ minutes.

5. Form the patties: Combine ground chuck and brisket with salt, pepper, and garlic. Divide into 4 portions (8 oz each). Shape into 4.5-inch patties sized to fit the focaccia squares, 3/4 inch thick, with a center dimple. Refrigerate 20 minutes.

6. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat with a thin film of neutral oil. Cook patties undisturbed 3–4 minutes. Flip; cook 2–3 more minutes. Target internal temperature 130–135°F for medium rare. Remove; tent with foil and rest 3–4 minutes.
7. While patties rest, tear burrata into generous pieces, allowing the creamy interior to spill slightly.
8. Toast focaccia bun halves cut-side down in olive oil in a skillet until golden and crisp, about 90 seconds.

9. Assemble: Spread tomato jam generously on both cut sides of the focaccia bun. Place the rested patty on the bottom bun. Arrange 3–4 slow-roasted Roma tomato halves over the patty. Place torn burrata pieces over the tomatoes, so the cream floods down over the beef. Add pickled red onion and shaved Parmigiano. Scatter fresh basil leaves. Drizzle with good olive oil. Finish with flaky sea salt and cracked pepper. Crown with the top bun.
10. Serve immediately, with extra tomato jam on the side.
